https://www.dw.com/en/romania-shuts-nucl.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ImuD The Cernavoda nuclear plant gathers all its cooling water from the Danube Image: Alex Nicodim/Anadolu/picture alliance Advertisement Romania shut down its lone nuclear power plant on Thursday, a rare move amid the drought that has caused record lows on the Danube River and other major waterways in Europe . The Danube is the sole source of cooling water for the Cernavoda plant, which usually generates around one-fifth of Romania's electricity. The power station has only been shut down once before, in 2023, again as a result of drought and a hot summer . Meanwhile, Hungary was scrambling to dam the Danube, as it tries to keep its Paks nuclear power plant at least running at the minimal levels that it has maintained in recent days, which are far below capacity. Attempts to divert more water to Cernavoda earlier this month didn't prevent a shutdown Image: Alex Nicodim/Anadolu/picture alliance What did the operator and authorities in Romania say about the shutdown? Romania's Nuclearelectrica company had already shut one of the two reactors at Cernavoda last month. On Thursday, it said it needed to shut the second "because of the significant and ongoing drop in the water level of the Danube River." The company tried earlier this month , with help from the Navy, to improve the plant's chances of staying operational. Most memorably, it blew up a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels and strategically deposited the rocks on the riverbed in a bid to direct more water to Cernavoda. But ultimately, continued dry weather and sinking water levels prompted the total shutdown. "We do not foresee a restart within the next 10 days," the plant director, Romeo Urjan, told the AFP news agency. Romania's Energy Ministry said it was procuring alternative power sources, including from wind power but also from energy imports, to try to ensure adequate supplies. Still it appealed to the public to consume responsibly. It warned that as a last resort, large industrial users would have to face restrictions in the evening hours to save electricity. Carmakers Ford and Dacia had already committed to pausing production until August 19 to save power. Earlier in August, the Romanian Navy detonated submerged rocks as part of a bid to funnel more water to the power plant Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance What is Hungary doing to try to prevent a similar shutdown of the Paks plant? Prime Minister Peter Magyar on Thursday visited Hungary's only nuclear power plant , the Paks facility that is also cooled by the Danube. "We have begun construction of the low weir that will permanently contribute to raising the Danube's water level," Magyar told reporters at the site, roughly 100 kilometers (about 60 miles) south of Budapest. Only one of Paks' four reactors is currently operational amid the drought. Nine days ago, the plant was at risk of a complete shutdown, but the government was able to abort those plans at the last moment as the Danube's levels ended up being a few millimeters higher than forecast. The unusually low river levels near the Paks plant are hard to miss at present Image: Robert Nemeti/Anadolu/picture alliance Under normal circumstances, the plant is responsible for around half of Hungary's electricity generation, and about one-third of its consumption. Before the completion of the weir, authorities plan to deliberately sink two 80-meter-long barges — placed end-to-end and perpendicular to the river's flow — to create an initial damming effect and raise the water level somewhat. Magyar said that Hungarian soldiers were working round the clock on the construction, and that it should be completed in the next four weeks. He said the project should elevate water levels in front of the Paks plant cooling system by more than a meter. The project might not be finished long before the summer starts to fade and the rains return, but the low water levels also provide a rare opportunity to undertake such construction projects relatively cheaply and easily. He warned such attacks threaten food security worldwide, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 5, 2026, 11:09 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha attends joint press conference with India’s External Affairs minister following their meeting in Kyiv on Aug. 3, 2026. (Photo by Genya SAVILOV / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Russia’s drone strike on a Turkish-owned cargo vessel carrying corn in the Black Sea, warning that civilian shipping routes urgently need stronger protection. The Royad Mammadov sank in Romania’s exclusive economic zone earlier on Monday, Oct. 5, after a fire broke out on board. President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement that two Russian drones had struck the ship, killing its captain, while the fate of another crew member remained unknown. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “Freedom of navigation cannot depend on whether Moscow decides to observe it on one day or another,” Sybiha said in a statement published on the Foreign Ministry’s website. Calls for pressure on Moscow Sybiha warned that attacks on vessels carrying Ukrainian agricultural exports could have devastating consequences for vulnerable communities in Africa, Asia and the Middle East that depend on imported food, potentially leading to acute food insecurity, malnutrition or even famine. Advertisement He said Ukraine had repeatedly offered concrete steps to make Black Sea navigation safer, but that Russia had responded by widening the reach of its attacks. “This trend will continue until the price of escalation becomes higher than the benefits that Moscow expects to get from it,” Sybiha said, calling for greater pressure on Russia, stronger protection for civilian shipping and accountability for attacks on vessels and their crews. Other Topics of Interest Russia Strikes Kharkiv With Guided Bombs Killing 6, Wounding 59, Including Children Two more bodies were found under the rubble of a sewing workshop, as rescuers continued searches through damaged buildings, with fires covering nearly 15,000 square meters (161,459 square feet). His remarks echoed Zelensky’s earlier statement that Russia “consistently chooses terror and the sinking of civilian vessels instead of normal navigation.” Sybiha described the attack as ‘cynical’ The attack, Sybiha said, proves particularly cynical given Turkey’s ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions, advance peace initiatives and ensure security in the region. The country has maintained diplomatic ties with both Moscow and Kyiv, despite being among the countries hit hardest by the escalating war at sea. Since late June, at least 25 Turkish-owned or Turkish-operated merchant vessels have been damaged or caught in the crossfire in the Black Sea. Advertisement Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan repeatedly urged both sides to agree on a mutual moratorium on attacks against commercial ships. In August, Ankara had begun restricting commercial transits through the Dardanelles toward the Black Sea, including routes to Russia’s port of Novorossiysk. Just a month later, Turkey sent a draft memorandum of understanding to Kyiv and Moscow aimed at formally halting strikes on commercial shipping and civilian port infrastructure. “We are trying to reach a conclusion. Frankly, both sides have demands and positions that are difficult to reconcile,” Fidan said on Sept. 20. So far, Moscow has rejected all ceasefire proposals. On Oct. 1, Bloomberg reported that Turkey and the UN had arranged new talks in Russia and Ukraine on a possible Black Sea ceasefire, aiming to bring together separate efforts to protect grain shipments as global food prices climb. According to a senior diplomat cited by the outlet, the meetings are set for early October, with the Swiss-based Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue acting as mediator. Ship sinking in Romania The Royad Mammadov had left Ukraine’s Danube port of Izmail with grain and was heading for Ravenna, Italy, according to Romanian media on Monday morning. Advertisement The Romanian Interior Ministry said 11 crew members were rescued and two deceased people were identified. Three injured sailors were airlifted for emergency medical treatment, while the remaining eight were taken aboard rescue vessels, Romanian broadcaster Digi24 reported. The ship sank while the rescue operation was still underway. The incident took place about 30 nautical miles south of the coastal village of Sfântu Gheorghe, outside Romania’s territorial waters. The 140-meter vessel sailed under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis, while shipping records list Turkey-based MG Shipping 5 Co Ltd as its registered owner. Romanian authorities have officially confirmed only a fire on board and have not determined its cause, attributed the incident to Russia or established the origin of any drone involved. Hours before the incident, Romania’s Defense Ministry said its radar had detected an airborne target near the border, east of the Ukrainian town of Vylkove. Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed to Romania for NATO air policing were scrambled, though the ministry said the target did not enter Romanian airspace. Authorities have not linked that incident to the fire on the ship. Advertisement Russia has not directly commented on the attack, though its Defense Ministry said it had struck two cargo vessels, the BBC reported.
